import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Green's Open Problem 64

*Reference:* [Ben Green's Open Problems](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#problem.64)

Do there exist infinitely many primes $p$ for which $p - 2$ has an odd number of prime factors,
counted with multiplicity?
-/

open ArithmeticFunction

open scoped ArithmeticFunction.Omega

namespace Green64

/--
Do there exist infinitely many primes $p$ for which $p - 2$ has an odd number of prime factors,
counted with multiplicity (i.e. $\Omega(p - 2)$ is odd)?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem green_64 :
    answer(sorry) ↔ {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ Odd (Ω (p - 2))}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/-- $5$ satisfies the condition: $5$ is prime and $5 - 2 = 3$ is prime, so $\Omega(3) = 1$ is odd. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem green_64_mem_five : 5 ∈ {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ Odd (Ω (p - 2))} := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, ?_⟩
  rw [show (5 : ℕ) - 2 = 3 by norm_num, cardFactors_apply_prime (by norm_num)]
  exact odd_one

/-- $7$ satisfies the condition: $7$ is prime and $7 - 2 = 5$ is prime, so $\Omega(5) = 1$ is odd. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem green_64_mem_seven : 7 ∈ {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ Odd (Ω (p - 2))} := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, ?_⟩
  rw [show (7 : ℕ) - 2 = 5 by norm_num, cardFactors_apply_prime (by norm_num)]
  exact odd_one

/-- $11$ does *not* satisfy the condition: although $11$ is prime, $11 - 2 = 9 = 3 ^ 2$ has
$\Omega(9) = 2$ prime factors, which is even. This shows the condition is non-trivial. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem green_64_not_mem_eleven : 11 ∉ {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ Odd (Ω (p - 2))} := by
  rintro ⟨-, hodd⟩
  rw [show (11 : ℕ) - 2 = 3 ^ 2 by norm_num, cardFactors_apply_prime_pow (by norm_num)] at hodd
  exact (by decide : ¬ Odd 2) hodd

/--
The same question as `green_64` but with $p - 1$ instead of $p - 2$.
Green notes this is "probably more natural".
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem green_64.variants.p_sub_one :
    answer(sorry) ↔ {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ Odd (Ω (p - 1))}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Green64

reformulations.difference: The set ranges over all natural-number primes and uses the totalized value Ω 0 = 0, without explicitly requiring p > 2 so that p - 2 is positive.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Odd (Ω n) implies Ω n > 0, and Mathlib proves Ω n > 0 iff n > 1. Thus every member already satisfies p - 2 > 1, hence p > 3. In particular, p = 2 and p = 3 are excluded. Adding p > 2 leaves the set exactly unchanged. The scratch file proves this set equality and the equivalence of its infinitude with the existence of qualifying primes above every natural bound.

sources_consulted: Ben Green, 100 Open Problems, Problem 64 and its complete comments, p. 31; current PDF dated 2026-01-30: https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#problem.64

Checked-out Mathlib: Mathlib/NumberTheory/ArithmeticFunction/Misc.lean (cardFactors and its zero, one, prime, prime-power, and factorization identities); Mathlib/NumberTheory/ArithmeticFunction/Defs.lean; Mathlib/Data/Nat/Factors.lean (primeFactorsList).
Local repository conventions and machinery: STATEMENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, AGENTS.md, FormalConjecturesUtil/Answer.lean, and FormalConjecturesUtil/Attributes/Basic.lean.
Supplied historical calibration material: /workspace/past_misformalizations/INDEX.md and pr03528.md, pr03604.md, pr03621.md, pr01138.md, pr05007.md, pr03884.md.
review.notes: All five declarations were checked. Green explicitly poses the main question and the p - 1 variant, with no recorded resolution in the cited source. Ω counts prime factors with multiplicity. Computations and independent Lean checks confirmed the boundary cases and all three numerical tests; the file's test proofs have no sorry dependencies. /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiles without errors or warnings.
